## Task Planning
This involves taking a project and dividing it into smaller individual tasks. It focuses on how these pieces of work are organized so they can be assigned and tracked through to completion.

### Work Breakdown structure
This strategy involves decomposing the overall project scope into smaller, more manageable, and hierarchically organized components called work packages. By systematically breaking down a project from the highest level of deliverables to individual tasks, teams can accurately estimate resource requirements, assign clear ownership, and establish a foundational framework for scheduling, budgeting, and tracking progress through to completion.

### Epics
This strategy involves defining large, overarching bodies of work that capture a broad project initiative or high-level feature set. Because these initiatives are too massive to be executed in a single iteration, they are systematically decomposed into smaller, actionable user stories or tasks. By grouping related work under an Epic, teams can track long-term progress, manage complex dependencies, and maintain a clear strategic connection between high-level project goals and day-to-day task execution.

### Task Dependency Mapping
This strategy involves identifying, documenting, and sequencing the logical relationships between project activities to establish the precise order of operations. By analyzing how tasks rely on one another—such as defining which activities must finish before a subsequent one can start—teams can construct a realistic workflow, isolate the critical path, and proactively manage scheduling risks or bottlenecks that could disrupt project completion.

### Working backwards to plan
This strategy begins by establishing a definitive, successful future outcome—such as a specific launch date or a fully realized deliverable—and planning sequentially in reverse to the present day. By starting with the end goal and working backward, teams identify the exact milestones, prerequisites, and critical dependencies required at each preceding stage. This methodology ensures that every planned task is directly tied to a necessary outcome, eliminating extraneous work and creating a highly targeted timeline for execution.

### Work packages
This strategy involves defining the lowest, most granular level of a Work Breakdown Structure (WBS) that can be reliably scheduled, budgeted, monitored, and assigned to a specific individual or team. A work package groups related tasks into a self-contained unit of work that yields a distinct, measurable deliverable. By managing project scope at this foundational level, teams can establish precise accountability, estimate costs and durations with greater accuracy, and track progress against a concrete set of acceptance criteria.

### Scope Relationship Diagrams
This strategy involves creating visual models that illustrate the structural, logical, and operational connections between different project components, features, and external dependencies. By mapping how scope elements interact with each other, teams can identify overlapping requirements, visualize data or process flows, and trace how changes to a single component might impact the broader system. This diagrammatic framework provides a holistic view of the project, helping stakeholders understand complex architectures and avoid unintended side effects when modifying the project scope.

### Estimating duration (?)
This strategy involves calculating the realistic timeframe required to complete individual tasks, work packages, or entire project phases. By utilizing methodologies such as analogous estimating (historical comparison), parametric estimating (statistical modeling), or three-point estimating (optimistic, pessimistic, and most likely scenarios), teams can move past guesswork to establish data-driven schedules. This framework accounts for resource availability, task complexity, and potential constraints, providing a foundational baseline for tracking project health and meeting target deadlines.

### Backlogs
This strategy involves maintaining a centralized, dynamically prioritized repository of all outstanding tasks, features, enhancements, and bug fixes required to fulfill the project scope. Serving as the single source of truth for the project team, this list is continuously refined and re-ordered based on shifting business value, stakeholder feedback, and resource capacity. By organizing work into a structured backlog, teams can smoothly transition upcoming priorities into immediate execution cycles while keeping long-term requirements visible and managed.

### Bucket size planning
This strategy involves categorizing tasks, features, or project requirements into high-level, distinct size classifications—such as T-shirt sizes (Small, Medium, Large, Extra Large) or time-based horizons (Now, Next, Later)—rather than assigning precise numerical estimations up front. By using these broad buckets, teams can rapidly gauge the relative effort, complexity, and scale of a large backlog without getting bogged down in premature micro-planning. This framework streamlines high-level capacity planning, manages stakeholder expectations early on, and helps prioritize resource allocation based on a rough order of magnitude.
